JSON: Name: tianjin_slaughterhouse_tax_inspection Title: Mixed-methods archival causal analysis of the effect of municipal slaughter-tax control on meat safety inspection efficacy in Republican Tianjin (1918–1949) Short Hypothesis: Increased municipal control over slaughter-tax revenue caused a measurable reduction in meat safety inspection rigor in Tianjin between 1918 and 1949, as evidenced by fewer recorded inspections per animal, greater incidence of confiscations without documented inspections, and more contemporaneous reports of smuggling and corruption. Related Work: Existing scholarship has documented the institutional emergence of government-run public abattoirs, the spread of hygienic modernity, and the role of veterinary knowledge and colonial medicine in early 20th-century Chinese treaty ports. Prior studies are primarily qualitative archival case studies or narrative institutional histories emphasizing planning, sanitary regulation texts, and professionalization of veterinary practice. Comparative work has focused on drivers for establishing abattoirs (disease fear, trade pressures) and on market/industrial dimensions of meat processing. Limitations of prior approaches include (1) scarce quantitative linkage between fiscal/taxation arrangements and inspection outcomes, (2) little use of cross-city comparative or counterfactual analyses to isolate causal effects, (3) limited exploitation of full-text archival corpora and computational text analysis to extract temporal trends, and (4) insufficient attention to measurable indicators of enforcement behavior (inspection counts, fines, confiscation dispositions) and public sentiment. This project addresses these gaps by combining structured archival coding, time-series causal inference, and computational content analysis. Abstract: Problem: Republican-era Tianjin established government-run slaughterhouses that combined mandatory veterinary inspection with municipal collection of slaughter taxes, but historical narratives suggest these institutions failed to deliver expected meat-safety outcomes. Approach: This study uses a mixed-methods archival pipeline that operationalizes inspection rigor, taxation control, and public distrust into time-series and document-level variables extracted from municipal archives, police records, Ministry regulations, and contemporary newspapers for Tianjin (1918–1949) and matched control cities. Methods include structured manual coding, automated full-text extraction, topic modeling, supervised classification of corruption/smuggling reports, and causal inference (difference-in-differences and instrumental-variable time-series regressions). Contribution: We provide the first reproducible, quantitative test of whether municipal fiscal control over slaughter taxation causally undermined meat-safety inspection efficacy in a major treaty port, and we furnish a validated computational toolkit for comparative archival governance studies. Expected outcome: Empirical estimates of the effect size of taxation control on inspection activity and public reporting, plus robustness checks and topic-level characterizations of corruption narratives, clarifying institutional mechanisms linking revenue incentives to public-service performance. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Digitized municipal archives for Tianjin (1918–1949): slaughterhouse logs (inspection counts, disposition codes), treasury records (slaughter-tax receipts, tax quotas), police interrogation records (smuggling arrests, fines), health bureau personnel/equipment inventories; (2) Full-text newspapers published in Tianjin (L'Impartial, Yishibao, Yongbao, Yishibao) 1910–1949; (3) Comparable archival corpora from at least two control cities (e.g., Beijing, Qingdao, Shanghai) with variation in whether taxation and inspection were administratively separated; (4) Auxiliary time-series: population, wartime occupation indicators, major epidemic/flood events, meat supply/shipment logs. Preprocessing: OCR + manual correction; date normalization; named-entity recognition for actors (abattoir staff, police, vendors); lexicon-based extraction of key event types (inspection, confiscation, fine, smuggling, bribe, equipment purchase). Feature construction (monthly resolution): inspections_per_month, animals_inspected_per_month, confiscations_without_inspection_count, fines_collected_amount, slaughter_tax_share_of_municipal_revenue, veterinarians_on_staff, equipment_index (microscopes, reagents), corruption_report_count (newspaper mentions), smuggling_arrests_count. Baselines: (A) Naive time-series regression predicting inspections_per_month from year and season only; (B) Model including public-health shocks (epidemic/flood) but excluding taxation variables; (C) Comparable-city model where tax/inspection functions are separated. Primary models: (1) Difference-in-differences (DiD) comparing Tianjin to control cities across policy-shock dates (e.g., 1925–1932 centralization of tax collection and 1928 national hygiene laws) with city and year fixed effects; (2) Time-series panel regression with AR(1) errors and covariates (epidemic indicators, wartime occupation, meat supply); (3) Instrumental-variables (IV) regression using exogenous shocks to municipal fiscal stress (e.g., flood damage receipts, sudden budget shortfalls) as instrument for increases in slaughter-tax centralization to estimate causal impact on inspections_per_month. Evaluation metrics (quantitative): coefficient estimates with 95% CIs, p-values, R-squared/AIC/BIC, impulse-response plots, placebo DiD tests on leads/lags, robustness to clustered standard errors by city-year. Text-analysis experiments: (A) Unsupervised topic modeling (LDA/NMF) on newspapers and police records to quantify prevalence over time of corruption/smuggling/food-safety topics; evaluate topic coherence (CV) and stability; (B) Supervised classification of corruption-smuggling mentions using annotated 1,000-document subset; evaluate precision, recall, F1 on held-out test set; (C) Ablation: retrain primary DiD/IV models after removing taxation variables, removing wartime years, and removing text-derived corruption_count to assess mediation. Comparison studies: (i) Direct compare effect sizes between Tianjin and each control city (separation-of-function vs combined-function), (ii) within-Tianjin comparison of periods with single-veterinarian staffing versus multi-veterinarian staffing. Reproducibility: release code for feature extraction, modeling notebooks, and annotated labels. Risk Factors and Limitations: Archival incompleteness and survivorship bias: key records (inspection logs, treasury ledgers) may be missing, selectively preserved, or uneven across periods and cities, biasing trend estimates. OCR and text-extraction errors: historical fonts, language variation, and damage will produce noisy features; downstream classifiers and topic models may inherit systematic error. Measurement validity: proxies (e.g., newspaper corruption mentions, confiscations_without_inspection) may imperfectly represent inspection rigor or actual corruption. Confounding and causal identification: contemporaneous shocks (war, occupation, food shortages, epidemics) correlate with both taxation policy and inspection activity, complicating causal inference; valid instruments may be weak. Small-N/time-series constraints: monthly or yearly resolution may yield limited effective sample size for robust IV/DiD estimates and increase Type I/II error risk. Temporal alignment and coding reliability: ambiguous dates and inconsistent event dating across sources limit precise matching and introduce measurement lag bias. Generalizability limits: findings from Tianjin (treaty-port, multi-jurisdictional governance) may not generalize to inland jurisdictions or different institutional contexts. Computational resource limits: large-scale OCR correction and manual annotation require significant human effort and storage; NLP models for classical Chinese or mixed-language archives may need specialized tooling. Legal/ethical constraints: access restrictions to some archival collections or restrictions on reproducing sensitive police records may limit dataset completeness.
